title: The nuclear atom and alpha-particle scattering

learning_outcomes.text: infer from the results of the α-particle scattering experiment the existence and small size of the nucleus
describe a simple model for the nuclear atom to include protons, neutrons and orbital electrons

external_knowledge: Electric charges with the same sign repel and charges with opposite signs attract.
Standard form can describe very small sizes.

prior_knowledge_summary: A positively charged object is repelled by another positively charged object.
A scientific model is tested by comparing its predictions with observations.
new_learning: Infer that most of an atom is empty space from the passage of most alpha particles through thin foil.
Infer a very small, positively charged, massive nucleus from rare large-angle alpha-particle deflections.
Describe an atom as a nucleus containing protons and neutrons with electrons orbiting outside the nucleus.
not_yet_taught: proton number and nucleon number bookkeeping

blocks.heading: A particle that seems to turn around
content: Imagine firing many tiny, fast, positively charged alpha particles at a sheet of metal foil. Almost every particle continues forward, yet a very small number turn through a large angle. How can a sheet that is easy for most particles to cross send a few almost back toward the source?
Make a prediction about what the inside of each atom must be like.

figure.purpose: Create the central contradiction between frequent transmission and rare strong deflection.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch. Show a narrow blue alpha-particle beam striking thin gold-coloured foil, many straight tracks, a few slightly bent tracks and one large-angle track. Use no atomic-model answer labels.
figure.alt_text: A beam reaches thin foil; most particle tracks continue forward while one turns through a large angle.

blocks.heading: Let each observation constrain the model
content: If most alpha particles pass straight through, most of the space inside an atom cannot contain matter concentrated enough to change their motion strongly. This observation suggests that most of an atom is empty space.

A few particles are deflected through small angles. They have passed near a charged part of an atom and experienced a weaker sideways repulsion. The rarer the close approach, the less often a large change of direction occurs.

figure.purpose: Link each common track observation to the emptiness inference.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper annotated path sketch through several widely spaced atoms. Show most alpha tracks crossing open space and one passing at moderate distance from a tiny centre with a slight curve. Label observation and inference in separate columns.
figure.alt_text: Most alpha particles cross open atomic space while one path curves slightly near a tiny centre.

blocks.heading: Rare large deflections reveal a small positive nucleus
content: An alpha particle is positively charged. A large change of direction needs a strong repulsive force, so the alpha particle must pass very close to a region of concentrated positive charge.

Only a very small fraction of particles come close enough for this to happen. The positively charged region must therefore occupy a very small fraction of the atom. The sharp turn also shows that the atom's mass is concentrated there, because a light spread-out region would not reverse a fast alpha particle. We call this tiny central region the nucleus.

figure.purpose: Show how closest approach changes the strength of repulsion and deflection.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison of three positive alpha paths past one tiny positive nucleus: distant and straight, nearer and slightly curved, very close and strongly turned. Use sparse plus signs and force arrows, with no equations.
figure.alt_text: Three positive alpha particles pass at different distances from a tiny positive nucleus and experience increasing deflection.

blocks.heading: Reason from a new set of results
content: Suppose 20 000 alpha particles strike a very thin foil. About 19 900 continue with little or no change, about 98 turn through modest angles and 2 turn through very large angles. Start with what is common: 19 900 out of 20 000 meet no concentrated obstacle, supporting the idea that most atomic volume is empty.

Now use what is rare: only 2 in 20 000 pass close enough to a concentrated positive region for a very strong repulsion. This supports a nucleus that is both very small and positively charged. The large change of motion supports the conclusion that most atomic mass is concentrated in that nucleus.
Independent check: one model explains both observations. A large diffuse positive region would deflect many particles, contradicting the overwhelmingly straight tracks.

figure.purpose: Teach the observation-to-inference chain without reproducing a practice question.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked reasoning layout with three rows: observation, physical cause, inference. Use simple tally icons for 19 900, 98 and 2 rather than a detailed chart. Highlight the contradiction check against a diffuse atom.
figure.alt_text: A reasoning table connects common straight paths and rare strong deflections to an empty atom and a small positive nucleus.

blocks.heading: Build the nuclear atom
content: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons. A proton has positive charge. A neutron has no net charge. Together these particles account for nearly all the mass of the atom in its tiny centre.

Electrons have negative charge and orbit outside the nucleus. They occupy the much larger region around it. Think of a large indoor arena with a grain-sized centre: the scale picture is not exact, but it helps separate the tiny nucleus from the much larger atomic volume.

figure.purpose: Identify the locations and charges of protons, neutrons and electrons in the simple nuclear model.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper cutaway atom sketch. Draw a tiny central nucleus enlarged in an inset with red protons marked plus and grey neutrons marked zero; show blue negative electrons on sparse orbital paths outside. Add a scale-warning note: not to scale.
figure.alt_text: A simple atom has protons and neutrons in a tiny nucleus and negative electrons orbiting outside.

blocks.heading: The nucleus is not large because it holds most of the mass
content: It feels reasonable to picture the nucleus as taking up most of the atom because it contains nearly all the mass. That mixes up mass with volume.

Scattering separates the two ideas. Rare large deflections show that the massive positive region is concentrated into a very small volume. Frequent straight paths show that the remaining atomic volume is mostly empty space. Small size and large concentration can be true together.

figure.purpose: Repair the confusion between where mass is concentrated and how much volume is occupied.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper two-column comparison. Left shows an incorrect large filled centre crossed out. Right shows a tiny dense centre inside a large faint atomic boundary, with separate bars for fraction of mass and fraction of volume.
figure.alt_text: A comparison distinguishes a tiny nucleus occupying little volume from its concentration of nearly all atomic mass.

blocks.heading: Observation, interaction, inference
content: Use a three-step route. First state the observation: most particles pass through, a few deflect slightly, or very few deflect greatly. Second identify the interaction: a positive alpha particle is repelled by concentrated positive charge. Third state only the supported inference.

Most straight paths imply that most of the atom is empty space. Rare large-angle paths imply a very small, positively charged nucleus in which nearly all the mass is concentrated. The simple nuclear model then places protons and neutrons in the nucleus and electrons orbiting outside.
Do not use later bookkeeping ideas such as nuclide notation or isotope labels yet. At this stage the goal is the structure and the evidence for it.

figure.purpose: Summarise the complete evidence-to-model reasoning route.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper flow diagram with three observation cards feeding three inference cards, then one simple nuclear-atom sketch. Keep wording short and use colour only to connect each observation to its inference.
figure.alt_text: A flow diagram links alpha-scattering observations to an atom that is mostly empty with a tiny positive massive nucleus.

visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

evidence_basis.p1_status: deferred by canonical lesson specification; no lesson assignment invented

misconceptions_addressed: The nucleus occupies most atomic volume because it contains nearly all atomic mass.
A straight alpha-particle path shows that the atom contains no matter.
next_lesson_can_assume: Most atomic volume is empty space.
The nucleus is very small, positively charged and contains nearly all atomic mass.
Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus and electrons orbit outside.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Radiation, decay equations or quark structure.
